Defend the thesis that scientific knowledge is best understood as provisional and fallible rather than as a body of established certainties. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) the history of science shows even well-confirmed theories — including Newtonian mechanics and classical thermodynamics — have been substantially revised or shown to hold only within bounded domains, establishing fallibilism as the empirically warranted epistemic stance; (2) the Duhem-Quine thesis shows no single hypothesis can be conclusively falsified in isolation, because any experimental outcome is consistent with auxiliary hypothesis revision, making scientific knowledge irreducibly holistic and defeasible; (3) the underdetermination of theory by evidence — any finite dataset is consistent with infinitely many competing theoretical frameworks — entails that empirical confirmation is always partial and certainty claims exceed what evidence can justify. Argue that moral responsibility requires a meaningful conception of agency that cannot be reduced to purely causal-mechanical description. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) ascriptions of moral responsibility presuppose that agents could have done otherwise — a counterfactual competence condition that deterministic causal chains cannot satisfy without importing a normative surplus the mechanistic framework does not contain; (2) reactive attitudes such as resentment, indignation, and gratitude are intelligible only within a framework that treats agents as sources of reasons-responsive action, not merely as nodes in causal networks; (3) compatibilist attempts to reconstruct agency within determinism succeed only by shifting the conceptual target — redefining 'could have done otherwise' in dispositional terms — which preserves the linguistic form of responsibility attribution while abandoning its normative substance. Defend the thesis that language fundamentally shapes — rather than merely expresses — the structure of human thought and cognition. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) cross-linguistic research on spatial cognition, color categorization, and number representation demonstrates systematic covariation between linguistic categories and non-linguistic cognitive performance, establishing that linguistic distinctions influence the granularity of conceptual representations; (2) language acquisition in early childhood does not merely label pre-existing content but actively restructures the child's representational system, evidenced by category-learning differences between linguistic and non-linguistic tasks in infants at the boundary of language acquisition; (3) even internal deliberative thought is partially constituted by linguistic representation, because the sequential and negation-permitting structure of natural language enables forms of reasoning that non-linguistic cognitive systems cannot support. Argue that aesthetic value cannot be coherently reduced to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience involves a claim to intersubjective validity — when we judge a work beautiful we implicitly call on others to agree, a normative dimension that a purely subjectivist framework cannot explain; (2) the practice of aesthetic criticism — with its apparatus of reasons, standards, and education — presupposes that aesthetic assessments are answerable to considerations beyond individual response, and that some responses are better-informed than others; (3) aesthetic relativism generates a regress: if every preference is equally valid, then the preference for pluralism over dogmatism is itself merely a preference, undermining the normative force of the relativist position from within. Defend the thesis that consciousness poses an explanatory challenge not fully addressed by any current physicalist or functionalist framework. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) the hard problem — why physical processes give rise to subjective experience at all — is conceptually distinct from the easy problems of explaining cognitive function; functional accounts address the latter but leave the former untouched because they explain what the brain does, not what it is like; (2) the conceivability of philosophical zombies — beings physically identical to conscious humans but lacking phenomenal experience — demonstrates that phenomenal consciousness is not logically entailed by physical description, meaning any identity between physical and phenomenal properties is contingent rather than necessary; (3) Mary's Room shows that complete physical knowledge does not entail complete knowledge of phenomenal properties, establishing that phenomenal facts are epistemically irreducible to physical facts even if ontological dualism is not entailed. Defend the thesis that distributive justice requires substantive attention to the pattern of outcomes, not merely to the fairness of the procedures that generate them. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) procedurally fair processes can and routinely do generate outcome distributions that are substantively unjust because they incorporate and amplify pre-existing structural inequalities including differential access to education and inherited wealth — procedural fairness is necessary but not sufficient; (2) Rawls's difference principle provides a principled criterion for evaluating outcome patterns: inequalities are justified only when they maximize the absolute position of the least-advantaged members of society; (3) the baseline problem — determining what counts as a fair starting point for procedurally legitimate exchange — cannot itself be resolved by procedural criteria, because any choice of baseline presupposes a prior substantive judgment about entitlement. Argue that large-scale technological systems reshape social structures and distributions of power in ways that resist effective governance through individual choice or conventional regulatory frameworks. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) technological systems exhibit what Winner calls 'politics built into design' — the material properties of platform architecture embed particular distributions of agency and dependency that are not visible to or revisable by individual users; (2) network externalities, switching costs, and data-compounding effects create structural lock-in that renders the theoretical availability of alternatives formally compatible with effective technological monopoly, making market competition insufficient as a governance mechanism; (3) the pace of technological deployment systematically outstrips the capacity of regulatory institutions to develop adequate oversight frameworks, creating a persistent governance gap that individual adaptation cannot close. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Defend the position that the meaning of a text is not fully determined by its author's original intentions. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) Wimsatt and Beardsley's intentional fallacy establishes that a literary work once composed becomes a linguistic artifact whose meanings are constituted by the conventions and interpretive practices of its language community, none of which are under the author's control; (2) the hermeneutic gap between what an author consciously intended and what a text semantically encodes is irreducible — authorial intention underdetermines textual meaning because the same linguistic tokens are consistent with multiple interpretive elaborations; (3) Barthes's 'death of the author,' read as a claim about interpretive authority rather than eliminativism, correctly identifies that the activation of textual meaning occurs in the reader's engagement with the text, drawing on competences that vary across readers and historical moments in ways original intention cannot anticipate. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Argue that democratic legitimacy requires more than majority rule or aggregated preference satisfaction. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) unrestricted majority rule is susceptible to the tyranny of the majority — the systematic exclusion of permanent minorities whose interests are structurally underrepresented in majoritarian aggregation; constitutional rights constraints and counter-majoritarian institutions are therefore a democratic requirement rather than a limitation on democracy; (2) deliberative democracy theorists including Habermas and Cohen establish that legitimate political decisions require the exchange of reasons under conditions of equal standing, mutual recognition, and openness to rational revision — conditions that bare majoritarianism neither requires nor ensures; (3) the epistemic argument for democracy is conditional on the quality of deliberation: majority decisions reached under systematic misinformation or manipulation lack the epistemic credentials that justify democratic authority, meaning legitimacy is not automatically conferred by procedural compliance. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Defend the thesis that rationality is not a universal context-independent capacity but is constitutively shaped by the cognitive, social, and institutional conditions in which it operates. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Argue that personal identity persists through psychological continuity rather than through physical or biological continuity. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Defend the thesis that mathematical objects possess a form of objectivity that is independent of human psychological or social construction. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

Argue that the replication crisis in psychology reveals a fundamentally institutional and incentive-structural problem, not merely a methodological one.
